# Fridge power station sizing

**Short answer:** for a typical full-size fridge, about **1,000 Wh** gets you most of a day, and **1,500-2,000 Wh** is the safer pick for a full 24 hours. For two days, plan on roughly 2,800 Wh or more. Check three things, not just battery size.

## 1. Surge watts (the spec that most often fails)
The compressor spikes briefly when it starts. Sources put the startup at roughly 1,000-1,300 W for a typical fridge, and up to about 2,400 W for large or older units. Look for a surge rating of at least **1,300 W**, and more if your fridge is big or old. Without it, the station trips at the first start, however large its battery is. ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator))

## 2. Continuous watts and waveform
A running fridge draws about 100-250 W, which almost any 1,000 W-class station covers. Choose a **pure sine wave** inverter, since compressor motors can run hot or fail to start on cheap modified-sine units. ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage))

## 3. Watt-hours
The compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time, so average draw is far below the label wattage. Estimates range from about 41 W (an ENERGY STAR model) to 60-70 W for a typical fridge. That works out to roughly 1,000-1,700 Wh per day once you allow for inverter losses and headroom. ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator), [HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/))

To personalize this, take the kWh/year figure from your fridge's yellow EnergyGuide label and multiply by 1,000, then divide by 8,760. That gives your average watts. Multiply by 24, then by about 1.4 for losses and headroom. Hot kitchens, ice makers, and frequent door openings push the number up.

## Options named in the sources
Prices change often, so confirm at checkout.

| Size | Example | Est. fridge runtime | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~1,000 Wh | Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 | ~17 hrs | About $499 per [HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/) |
| ~1,150 Wh | BLUETTI AC180 | Most of a day | 1,800 W output, 2,700 W peak; $399-699 recently seen per [BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) |
| ~2,000 Wh | Anker SOLIX S2000 | About a day or more | 1,500 W output, 3,000 W peak; $699.99 after coupon per [Anker](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) |
| ~2,050 Wh | [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l) | ~33 hrs | $899, or $854.05 with code AFF5OFF per [Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l); expandable to 8,192 Wh |

Only the AC200L has a direct buy link in my results. For the others, the links go to the guide pages that list them.

## Tips
- Keep the door closed. Food is considered unsafe after about 4 hours above 40°F with the door shut. ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/))
- If you also want to run a router, lights, or a freezer, add their watt-hours.
- Skip compact units under about 300 Wh. They typically fail the surge check.
- Test the setup before an outage.

If you tell me your fridge's size or EnergyGuide kWh/year, and how many hours or days you want to cover, I can narrow this to one pick.
